title: Ancient pollen tells the story of ice age footprints
summary:
Some of the oldest human footprints in North America are at White Sands National Park in New Mexico. A new study adds more proof that they were made during the last ice age, about 23,500 to 21,700 years ago.

For a long time, many scientists thought people first came to North America about 16,000 to 12,000 years ago. So these footprints surprised them, and scientists have argued about their age for years.

Researchers from the University of Arizona studied hundreds of thousands of tiny pollen grains from the tracks. Pollen is a powder made by plants. It showed what plants grew there and what the weather was like.

The land changed fast. In just a few decades, evergreen forests turned into plains with oak and sage. A giant lake rose and shrank for about 1,500 years and then dried up.

People walked there alongside mammoths, giant sloths and dire wolves, said scientist Jessica Tierney.
why_it_matters: Clues as tiny as pollen can tell us when people first lived in North America and how they handled big changes in nature.

keywords.explanation: An ice age is a long time when Earth was much colder and big sheets of ice covered land.
Pollen is a fine powder made by plants.
Plains are large, flat areas of land with few trees.
Mammoths were huge, hairy animals related to elephants that lived long ago.
Sloths are slow-moving animals, and giant ground sloths lived long ago.

background_read: Long ago, during the last ice age, Earth was much colder and many animals that are now gone, like mammoths, were alive.
Footprints pressed into soft mud can harden and stay hidden for thousands of years.
Tiny pollen grains last a long time, so scientists can use them to learn which plants grew in a place long ago.
